A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same diffusion-trajectory origin-attribution study. All nine pages of v2 and twelve pages of v3, including Appendices A–B and A–C respectively, support comparison of the text, equations, tables and figures despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V2 reports original membership-inference, model-attribution and origin-attribution experiments, feature ablations, an extraction case study and trajectory-based CIFAR-10 classification.

after.justification: V3 retains original attribution and classification results and adds membership-inference experiments varying data budgets and random splits, including CIFAR-100 evaluation.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same time-step loop, independent noise sampling, denoising losses and input/parameter gradient-norm features. The linear classifier and deterministic PIA adaptation are also retained. V3 clarifies and relocates their descriptions without establishing a procedural change.

E1.justification: V3 adds CIFAR-100 membership-inference evaluation, using CIFAR-100 validation data as the external set (Figure 5, Table 4 and Appendix A). Existing CIFAR-10/CIFAR-10.1 and CelebA-HQ/FFHQ coverage, attribution tasks and CIFAR-10 object classification remain. This is a limited benchmark expansion within the existing image domain.

E2.justification: The evaluated MIA comparators remain the model-blind ResNet18 baseline, Matsumoto et al., PIA and GSA2; MA and OA retain the model-blind comparator. Pang et al. (2024) becomes Pang et al. (2025), referring to the same GSA2 work. Newly cited approaches are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Table 3 replaces v2's 100- and 125-query sampling studies within steps 0–499 with 250-query comparisons spanning steps 0–999. V3 also introduces variable development budgets, TPR at 0.1% FPR and evaluation with potentially object-imbalanced random splits. These substantially extend the evaluation design; default classifier hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds data-budget sensitivity analyses against GSA2 in Figures 4–5 and split-robustness analysis in Table 4, testing dependence on limited and potentially imbalanced development data. The temporal-sampling ablation is substantially revised. Existing feature ablations, trajectory visualizations, extraction examples and object-classification analysis are retained.

E5.justification: V2 does not report repeated-split counts or dispersion for attack-performance estimates. V3 Table 4 reports ten random splits, individual TPRs, means and standard deviations for both methods on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. This introduces a substantive assessment of experimental variability, without establishing how many runs underlay v2's scores.

E6.justification: V3 adds budget-dependent results and random-split outcomes; Table 4 reports CIFAR-100 mean TPR at 1% FPR of 9.4 for the proposed method versus 2.6 for GSA2. Table 3 reports replacement results under different query settings, and v2's coarse-step MIA result row is omitted. MA, OA, feature-ablation and object-classification scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, denoising-loss formulation, trajectory features and linear classification mathematics retain their substance. V3's numbered Goldilocks conjecture restates the hypothesis already discussed in v2. The expanded threat-model discussion clarifies existing access assumptions; no new proof or substantive theoretical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The trajectory-based OA contribution remains, but v3's introduction and Section 7.2 add a central position that conventional MIAs cannot prove training membership and should be redirected toward data extraction. This substantially reframes their evidential role and the recommended research objective. The global-trajectory and first white-box DDPM-attribution claims already appear in v2.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly acknowledges the strong, nonstandard member-data assumption and the absence of a theoretical basis for gradient features. It adds substantive concerns about opaque foundation-model pretraining, corruption robustness and false-attribution harms. Conversely, Appendix B removes v2's hypothesis that stochastic features help by acting as a regularizer.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds GPU and operating-system details, explicit normalization and object-balancing information, and the hyperparameter-selection criterion. The numerical classifier settings are unchanged. V3 also removes the explicit DDPM implementation and SSCD repository links supplied in v2, creating a limited loss of implementation traceability.

R1.justification: V3 adds substantive engagement with Zhang et al. (2025) on membership evidence and Liu et al. (2025) on foundation-based attribution, alongside additional MIA references. It substantially revises positioning around surrogate assumptions, data extraction and direct diffusion attribution. Publication updates for existing works, including GSA2, do not constitute new cited research.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the narrative are rewritten. V2's method–experiments structure becomes separate threat-model, MIA-critique, Goldilocks, OA and recommendation sections. Implementation information moves into a new Appendix A, the previous two appendix analyses merge into Appendix B, and Appendix C adds broader-impact discussion.

P2.justification: V3 changes the predominantly two-column layout to a single-column NeurIPS format and extensively relocates and resizes the six original figures. It adds Figures 4–5 and Table 4, restructures Table 3 and separates the main MIA baseline display from retained proposed-method results in the appendix. Captions and table placement are extensively revised.

improvement.justification: The new budget and split analyses, particularly Table 4's variability reporting, make the empirical evidence more assessable. Explicit assumptions and qualified gradient explanations also improve clarity. These gains strengthen evidence within the controlled DDPM setting while leaving the stated MA failures unresolved. Removing implementation links and the coarse-step MIA row loses some useful detail, but the overall balance is a limited improvement.
